'''David E. Clemmer''' (February 23, 1965, [[Alamosa, Colorado]]) is an analytical chemist and the Distinguished Professor and Robert and Marjorie Mann Chair of Chemistry at [[Indiana University Bloomington|Indiana University]] in [[Bloomington, Indiana]], where he leads the Clemmer Group.<ref name="Bloomington">{{cite web|title=Clemmer Group Prof. David E. Clemmer|url=http://www.indiana.edu/~clemmer/Group%20Members/David.php|website=Indiana University Bloomington|access-date=26 April 2017}}</ref>   Clemmer develops new scientific instruments for [[Ion-mobility spectrometry|ion mobility mass spectrometry]] (IMS/MS), including the first instrument for nested ion-mobility [[Time-of-flight mass spectrometry|time-of-flight]] mass spectrometry.<ref name="Waters">{{cite web|title=Professor David Clemmer, Indiana University|url=http://www.waters.com/waters/en_US/Professor-David-Clemmer,-Indiana-University/nav.htm?cid=134714878&locale=en_US|website=Waters The Science of What's Possible|access-date=26 April 2017|archive-date=23 June 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130623054903/http://www.waters.com/waters/en_US/Professor-David-Clemmer,-Indiana-University/nav.htm?cid=134714878&locale=en_US|url-status=dead}}</ref>  He has received a number of awards, including the Biemann Medal in 2006 "for his pioneering contributions to the integration of ion mobility separations with a variety of mass spectrometry technologies."<ref name="Bierbaum"/>

== Early life and education ==
Clemmer was born on February 23, 1965, to Ed Clemmer, an artist, and his wife MaryAnn, a teacher, of [[Alamosa, Colorado]].<ref name="Relyea"/>  He attended [[Adams State College]], where he originally majored in music, before changing to science.<ref name="Relyea"/> He received his B.S. in chemistry with honors in 1987.  He then attended the [[University of Utah]], receiving his Ph.D. in physical chemistry in 1992.<ref name="Honors">{{cite web|title=University Honors & Awards: Honoree David E. Clemmer|url=https://honorsandawards.iu.edu/search-awards/honoree.shtml?honoreeID=2081|website=Indiana University Bloomington|access-date=28 April 2017|archive-date=27 April 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150427015843/https://honorsandawards.iu.edu/search-awards/honoree.shtml?honoreeID=2081|url-status=dead}}</ref> His thesis advisor was [[Peter B. Armentrout]],<ref name="Waters"/> with whom he studied transition metal ions in gaseous reactions.<ref name="Bierbaum"/>

==Career==
During 1992–1993, Clemmer was a postdoctoral fellow in Japan, supported by the Japan Society for the Promotion of Science Fellowship at the [[Himeji Institute of Technology]]. He worked with Kenji Honma on electron transfer mechanisms<ref name="Honma">{{cite journal|last1=Honma|first1=Kenji|last2=Clemmer|first2=David E.|title=The Importance of Electron Transfer Mechanism in Reactions of Neutral Transition Metal Atoms|journal=Laser Chemistry|date=1995|volume=15|issue=2–4|pages=209–220|doi=10.1155/1995/25319|doi-access=free}}</ref> and reactions of excited-state metal atoms and gaseous molecules.<ref name="Bierbaum"/>
From 1993 to 1995, Clemmer was a postdoctoral research associate at [[Northwestern University]], where he worked with Martin F. Jarrold,<ref name="Bierbaum"/> studying [[protein folding]] and protein conformation in the gas phase, using techniques such as [[Ion-mobility spectrometry]].<ref name="Jarrold">{{cite journal|last1=Clemmer|first1=David E.|last2=Jarrold|first2=Martin F.|s2cid=16681465|title=Ion Mobility Measurements and their Applications to Clusters and Biomolecules|journal=Journal of Mass Spectrometry|date=June 1997|volume=32|issue=6|pages=577–592|doi=10.1002/(SICI)1096-9888(199706)32:6<577::AID-JMS530>3.0.CO;2-4|bibcode=1997JMSp...32..577C }}</ref><ref name="Hudgins">{{cite journal|last1=Clemmer|first1=David E.|last2=Hudgins|first2=Robert R.|last3=Jarrold|first3=Martin F.|title=Naked Protein Conformations: Cytochrome c in the Gas Phase|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|date=October 1995|volume=117|issue=40|pages=10141–10142|doi=10.1021/ja00145a037|bibcode=1995JAChS.11710141C |url=http://www.indiana.edu/~clemmer/Publications/pubs/pub%20031.pdf|access-date=1 May 2017|archive-date=21 April 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160421054220/http://www.indiana.edu/~clemmer/Publications/pubs/pub%20031.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>

In 1995, Clemmer joined the Department of Chemistry at Indiana University.<ref name="Bierbaum"/> He served as chair of the Chemistry Department from 2002 to 2006.<ref name="Utah"/> He is a full professor, and holds the Robert and Marjorie Mann Chair of Chemistry, to which he was named in 2002.<ref name="Bierbaum"/><ref name="Honors"/> He has published more than 230 papers.<ref name="Bloomington"/>

Among those who have influenced him, he includes [[Michael T. Bowers]], [[Jesse L. Beauchamp]], [[R. Graham Cooks]], [[Scott A. McLuckey]], [[Fred McLafferty]], Evan R. Williams, Joseph A. Loo, [[Vicki Wysocki]], and [[Julie A. Leary]].<ref name="Waters"/> His graduate students have included [[Renã A. S. Robinson]], Stephen Valentine, Cherokee Hoaglund-Hyzer,<ref name="Hinnefeld"/> and Catherine Srebalus Barnes.<ref name="Connelley-Eskine"/>

== Research ==
[[File:Ion mobility spectrometry diagram.svg |thumb|right|300px| Drift tube for ion mobility spectrometry]]
Clemmer is particularly interested in studying the structural characterization and conformational dynamics of complex low-symmetry systems. Clemmer develops scientific instruments and methods for the examination of [[Biomolecule|biomolecular structure]] and complex biomolecular mixtures in the gas phase using ion-mobility spectrometry.<ref name="Connelley-Eskine"/>

Ion mobility methods separate ions into different groups based on their ability to move through an electrically charged buffer gas.  This enables complex mixtures to be differentiated in ways that could not be achieved by mass spectrometry alone. Even minute amounts of compounds can be distinguished and differentially examined according to characteristics such as size, shape and charge as well as mass.<ref name="Waters"/>

Clemmer has helped to establish ion mobility as both a powerful tool and a field of research through his "thorough studies" and "revolutionary instrumental methods".<ref name="Bierbaum"/>  In early work, Clemmer and Jarrold used long drift tubes with non-clustering gas atmospheres to increase the resolving power of ion-mobility spectrometry.<ref name="Eiceman">{{cite book|last1=Eiceman|first1=G.A.|last2=Karpas|first2=Z.|last3=Hill, Jr.|first3=H.H.|title=Ion mobility spectrometry|date=2014|publisher=CRC|location=Boca Raton, Fla.|isbn=9781439859971|pages=30–31|edition=Third}}</ref> Clemmer's work on gas-phase separation methods for [[Ion-mobility spectrometry–mass spectrometry|ion mobility-mass spectrometry]] (IM-MS) and their application to the structural analysis of intact proteins is considered a "particularly important milestone" in the application of IM-MS to the examination of biomolecular structures.<ref name="McLean">{{cite journal|last1=McLean|first1=John A.|title=The mass-mobility correlation redux: The conformational landscape of anhydrous biomolecules|journal=Journal of the American Society for Mass Spectrometry|date=October 2009|volume=20|issue=10|pages=1775–1781|doi=10.1016/j.jasms.2009.06.016|pmid=19646898|doi-access=|bibcode=2009JASMS..20.1775M |s2cid=205703562 }}</ref><ref name="Shelimov">{{cite journal|last1=Shelimov|first1=K.B.|last2=Clemmer|first2=D.E.|last3=Hudgins|first3=R.R.|last4=Jarrold|first4=M.F.|s2cid=9163743|title=Protein Structure in Vacuo: The Gas Phase Conformations of BPTI and Cytochrome c|journal=J. Am. Chem. Soc.|date=1997|volume=119|issue=9|pages=2240–2248|doi=10.1021/ja9619059|bibcode=1997JAChS.119.2240S }}</ref><ref name="Ibrahim">{{cite journal|last1=Ibrahim|first1=Yehia M.|last2=Baker|first2=Erin S.|last3=Danielson|first3=William F.|last4=Norheim|first4=Randolph V.|last5=Prior|first5=David C.|last6=Anderson|first6=Gordon A.|last7=Belov|first7=Mikhail E.|last8=Smith|first8=Richard D.|title=Development of a new ion mobility time-of-flight mass spectrometer|journal=International Journal of Mass Spectrometry|date=February 2015|volume=377|pages=655–662|doi=10.1016/j.ijms.2014.07.034|pmc=4501404|pmid=26185483|bibcode=2015IJMSp.377..655I }}</ref> Clemmer and his colleagues have developed at least a dozen different configurations combining modular components for ion-mobility with mass spectrometry instruments.<ref name="Waters"/><ref name="Instruments">{{cite web|title=Clemmer Group Development of New Ion Mobility Instrumentation|url=http://www.indiana.edu/~clemmer/Research/Early%20Work/Development.html|website=Indiana University|access-date=2 May 2017}}</ref>  These include combining ion mobility with [[Time-of-flight mass spectrometry]] (TOF).<ref name="Hoaglund">{{cite journal|last1=Hoaglund|first1=Cherokee S.|last2=Valentine|first2=Stephen J.|last3=Sporleder|first3=C. Ray|last4=Reilly|first4=James P.|last5=Clemmer|first5=David E.|title=Three-Dimensional Ion Mobility/TOFMS Analysis of Electrosprayed Biomolecules|journal=Anal. Chem.|date=1998|volume=70|issue=11|pages=2236–2242|url=http://www.indiana.edu/~clemmer/Publications/pubs/pub%20049.pdf|access-date=1 May 2017|doi=10.1021/ac980059c|pmid=9624897|bibcode=1998AnaCh..70.2236H |archive-date=10 August 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170810024825/http://www.indiana.edu/~clemmer/Publications/pubs/pub%20049.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="Henderson">{{cite journal|last1=Henderson|first1=Sheila C.|last2=Valentine|first2=Stephen J.|last3=Counterman|first3=Anne E.|last4=Clemmer|first4=David E.|title=ESI/Ion Trap/Ion Mobility/Time-of-Flight Mass Spectrometry for Rapid and Sensitive Analysis of Biomolecular Mixtures|journal=Anal. Chem.|date=1999|volume=71|issue=2|pages=291–301|url=http://www.indiana.edu/~clemmer/Publications/pubs/pub%20049.pdf|access-date=1 May 2017|doi=10.1021/ac9809175|pmid=9949724|bibcode=1999AnaCh..71..291H |archive-date=10 August 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170810024825/http://www.indiana.edu/~clemmer/Publications/pubs/pub%20049.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="Myung">{{cite journal|last1=Myung|first1=Sunnie|last2=Lee|first2=Young Jin|last3=Moon|first3=Myeong Hee|last4=Taraszka|first4=John|last5=Sowell|first5=Rena|last6=Koeniger|first6=Stormy|last7=Hilderbrand|first7=Amy E.|last8=Valentine|first8=Stephen J.|last9=Cherbas|first9=Lucy|last10=Cherbas|first10=Peter|last11=Kaufmann|first11=Thomas C.|last12=Miller|first12=David F.|last13=Mechref|first13=Yehia|last14=Novotny|first14=Milos V.|last15=Ewing|first15=Michael A.|last16=Sporleder|first16=C. Ray|last17=Clemmer|first17=David E.|title=Development of High-Sensitivity Ion Trap Ion Mobility Spectrometry Time-of-Flight Techniques: A High-Throughput Nano-LC-IMS-TOF Separation of Peptides Arising from a Protein Extract|journal=Analytical Chemistry|date=October 2003|volume=75|issue=19|pages=5137–5145|doi=10.1021/ac030107f|pmid=14708788|url=https://works.bepress.com/youngjin-lee/6/|access-date=1 May 2017|url-access=subscription}}</ref> They also developed the first instrument for nested ion-mobility [[Time-of-flight mass spectrometry|time-of-flight]] mass spectrometry.<ref name="Waters"/><ref name="Honors"/>

Such equipment allows researchers to learn more about both the structures and the conformational dynamics of systems.<ref name="Lanucara">{{cite journal|last1=Lanucara|first1=Francesco|last2=Holman|first2=Stephen W.|last3=Gray|first3=Christopher J.|last4=Eyers|first4=Claire E.|s2cid=2512242|title=The power of ion mobility-mass spectrometry for structural characterization and the study of conformational dynamics|journal=Nature Chemistry|date=21 March 2014|volume=6|issue=4|pages=281–294|doi=10.1038/nchem.1889|pmid=24651194|bibcode=2014NatCh...6..281L }}</ref> Clemmer has identified fundamental relationships between charge states and structures, and has shown that a single charge state can exist in more than one conformation in gaseous states.<ref name="Bierbaum"/> Such techniques can be used for the study of both proteins and peptides.<ref name="Gross">{{cite book|last1=Gross|first1=Michael L.|last2=Chen|first2=Guodong|last3=Pramanik|first3=Birendra N.|title=Protein and peptide mass spectrometry in drug discovery|date=2012|publisher=Wiley|location=Hoboken, N.J.|isbn=978-0-470-25817-0|pages=202–203|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6TRGqsQConQC&pg=PT202}}</ref><ref name="Bierbaum"/> In early work, Clemmer showed that multiple conformations of the [[hemeprotein]] [[cytochrome c]] could be differentiated based on their mobilities.<ref name="Hoaglund-Hyzer">{{cite journal|last1=Hoaglund-Hyzer|first1=Cherokee S.|last2=Counterman|first2=Anne E.|last3=Clemmer|first3=David E.|title=Anhydrous Protein Ions|journal=Chem. Rev.|date=1999|volume=99|issue=10|pages=3037–3079|url=http://www.iub.edu/~clemmer/Publications/pubs/pub%20054.pdf|access-date=1 May 2017|doi=10.1021/cr980139g|pmid=11749510|archive-date=9 February 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180209003110/http://www.iub.edu/~clemmer/Publications/pubs/pub%20054.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> In addition, the mobility of different chiral isomers was related to their protein folding.<ref name="Shvartsburg">{{cite book|last1=Shvartsburg|first1=Alexandre A.|title=Differential Ion Mobility Spectrometry: Nonlinear Ion Transport and Fundamentals of FAIMS |date=2008|publisher=CRC Press|location=Boca Raton, Fla.|pages=25–26}}</ref> More recent techniques enable researchers to track transitions in the conformations of macromolecular ions during the gas phase. A short pulse of ions is introduced into a drift tube by electrospray ionization. Structures separate based on differences in their mobilities. By exposing specific states to energizing collisions, new structures can be established and tracked through different conformational changes. Changes in conformation during the gas-phase data can then be mapped back to the original populations of structures. In this way, researchers can understand the possible pathways between structures.<ref>{{cite web|title=Spectroscopy Society of Pittsburgh January Meeting, 2013|url=http://www.ssp-pgh.org/january-2013-meeting/|website=Spectroscopy Society of Pittsburgh|access-date=2 May 2017|archive-date=4 July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200704090950/http://www.ssp-pgh.org/january-2013-meeting/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Understanding how protein folding occurs in three-dimensional molecules is one of biology's enduring problems. Proteins with different shapes often have very different biological activity and medical usefulness.<ref name="Honors"/> Clemmer's work has applications in the life sciences for understanding the conformation of structures in large protein complexes,<ref name="Honors"/> profiling the plasma proteome,<ref name="McLean"/> examining the role of proteins and protein folding in neurodegenerative diseases,<ref name="Honors"/> identifying possible cancer-related markers in blood, urine, or saliva,<ref name="Relyea"/> and increasing the efficiency of drug-discovery.<ref name="MIT35"/>  Ion mobility-mass spectrometry techniques also allow the measurement and correlation of a wide variety of different characteristics simultaneously in a single analysis. Researchers can use these techniques to examine complex biological samples for [[lipidomics]], [[proteomics]], [[glycomics]], and [[metabolomics]] information.<ref name="McLean"/>

==Companies==
Clemmer is a co-founder of ''Beyond Genomics'', a systems biology company, and the founder of ''Predictive Physiology and Medicine'', a biotechnology company specializing in [[personalized medicine]].<ref name="Relyea"/>

==Hobbies==
In addition to playing several instruments, Clemmer enjoys running marathons.<ref name="Waters"/>
